title: Tumor-Immune Microenvironment of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: Implications for Immune-Based Prevention and Therapy.
authors: Perea José; González-Sanmartín María; Coiras Mayte; Ogino Shuji
abstract: Early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC), typically defined as colorectal cancer diagnosed before 50 years of age, is increasing in incidence worldwide and exhibits distinctive clinical, molecular, and environmental features compared with later-onset (LOCRC) disease. However, the tumor-immune microenvironment (TiME) of EOCRC and its implications for prevention and therapy remain poorly characterized. In this review, we synthesize current evidence on the TiME of EOCRC and contrast it with that of conventional LOCRC. We first discuss global features of the EOCRC immune landscape, including innate and adaptive immune composition, functional states, and spatial organization, highlighting areas where apparent age-related differences reflect true biology versus confounding by tumor site, stage, or mismatch repair (MMR) status. We then examine immunogenomic and epigenomic determinants-such as MMR deficiency distribution, microbial mutational signatures, chromosomal instability, and age-conditioned methylation programs-that shape neoantigen landscapes, antigen presentation, and immune evasion in younger patients. Next, we review microbiome-driven immunomodulation, focusing on dysbiosis, genotoxic bacteria, and early-life and young-adult exposures as joint modifiers of mucosal immunity and tumor development. Finally, we explore how these insights inform immune-based prevention (risk stratification, screening, diet and microbiome interventions, and chemoprevention) and immunotherapy strategies, including checkpoint blockade and rational combinations in the predominant microsatellite-stable EOCRC population.

title: Nutrient control enables metabolic reconstruction of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG and analysis of secretions.
authors: Richmond Gracelyn R; Cunha Emanuel; Kelly Libusha; Dias Óscar; Chang Roger L
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) is an important gut commensal bacterial strain that has been extensively studied in both industrial and health settings. Despite its long history of study, a high-quality genome-scale metabolic network model (GEM) for LGG has yet to be reconstructed. Only automatically generated draft models have been published, which have notoriously limited functional accuracy. Furthermore, comprehensive nutrient requirements have not been established for well-controlled in vitro studies. Here, we present the first curated GEM for LGG using a new approach for reconstruction and validation that leverages multiple automatically generated draft models, applied study literature, and high-throughput defined media experiments. In addition, our results include a series of chemically defined media, extensive single-component nutrient dropout growth data, insights from in silico and in vitro experiments into secretion products, lactate, and indole-3-carboxaldehyde, a minimal medium, and in silico characterization of LGG's nutrient requirements. Our approach for developing interdisciplinary research tools for LGG metabolism comprises a new framework that could be applied to many understudied microorganisms, particularly useful in studying bacteria within the human microbiome.
IMPORTANCE: This study provides an important foundation for understanding how the beneficial gut bacterium Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) grows and interacts with its environment. Although LGG is one of the most widely studied probiotic bacteria, used in both health and industrial applications, a reliable tool for simulating its metabolic behavior and a clear understanding of its nutritional needs is lacking. By developing the first manually curated metabolic model of LGG and validating it through extensive laboratory experiments, this study provides new understanding of LGG's requirements and capabilities for utilizing nutrients and resources to investigate its metabolism. Completely chemically defined growth media and associated single-component dropout growth effects are also presented, and pathways for production of important compounds influencing human health are explored. The methods developed in this work also provide a framework for studying other poorly characterized microbes, helping advance research on the human microbiome and its role in health and disease.

title: Preventing Clostridioides difficile Infection and Recurrence: Practical Strategies for Clinical Practice.
authors: Axelrad Jordan E; Allegretti Jessica R
abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare utilization worldwide. Although advances in antimicrobial stewardship and infection prevention have reduced healthcare-associated disease in some settings, the incidence of community-associated CDI and the persistent burden of recurrent CDI (rCDI) continue to pose substantial clinical challenges. Because recurrent disease is fundamentally driven by persistent disruption of the intestinal microbiome and loss of colonization resistance, prevention has emerged as the central strategy for reducing long-term disease burden. This review summarizes contemporary evidence supporting prevention of both incident and rCDI, emphasizing practical approaches for gastroenterologists. Primary prevention centers on minimizing modifiable risk factors through antimicrobial stewardship, infection prevention and control, diagnostic stewardship to distinguish colonization from infection, and strategies to preserve the intestinal microbiome. For patients with CDI, we review evidence supporting extended antibiotic regimens, oral vancomycin prophylaxis during subsequent systemic antibiotic exposure, and microbiome restoration therapies, including conventional fecal microbiota transplantation and US Food and Drug Administration-approved microbiota-based therapies, which have transformed secondary prevention by restoring microbial diversity and colonization resistance. Special consideration is given to populations at particularly high risk for recurrence, including older adults, immunocompromised individuals, transplant recipients, and patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Finally, we discuss emerging preventive strategies, including precision risk stratification, microbiome- and metabolome-based biomarkers, bile acid modulation, and approaches targeting asymptomatic colonization. Together, these advances signal a paradigm shift from treating CDI episodes to implementing personalized preventive strategies that interrupt the cycle of recurrent disease and improve long-term patient outcomes.

title: Early-life bovine respiratory virome analysis reveals phage-driven adaptation and cross-host evolutionary signatures.
authors: Wang Yue; Kim Hanbeen; Malmuthuge Nilusha; Zhou Mi; Chen Yanhong et al.
abstract: Past outbreaks of zoonotic viral infections highlight the importance of understanding respiratory virome ecology. As major food-producing animals with frequent human contact, cattle represent a critical host at the human-animal interface; however, the early-life establishment of their respiratory virome and its evolutionary connections to viruses from other hosts remain underexplored. Here, we longitudinally profile the upper respiratory tract (URT) virome of beef calves from birth to weaning using an optimized viral enrichment procedure and metagenomic workflow. Viral communities exhibited increased richness and turnover, reflecting ecological structuring during early life. Temperate phages dominate the URT phage community and share virulence- and mobility-associated genes with bacterial hosts, likely contributing to host adaptation and colonization persistence. Vertebrate-associated viruses emerge after the first week of life. Targeted reassembly from bovine URT viromes recovers near-complete betacoronavirus-like (CoV-D180) and adenovirus-like (AdV-D56) genomes positioned phylogenetically between bovine and human viral lineages. Competitive mapping of bovine-derived CoV-D180 and AdV-D56 to human respiratory metatranscriptomic datasets reveals genome-specific, regionally structured coverage patterns distinct from reference viruses, supporting shared sequence features in conserved genomic regions across host-associated viral lineages. Collectively, these findings reveal early-life assembly dynamics of the bovine respiratory virome and highlight cross-host signatures in a One Health framework.
